1797.dq: Barring the consideration of clitics, main word stress is final and there is no evidence of secondary stress. (p.591; the authors separately distinguish 'phrase-level H tones—which also dock to final stressed syllables', fn.4, p.594-595, i.e. word stress is kept apart from phrasal intonation.)
1797.prule: Main word stress is final by default, quantity-insensitive ('syllable quantity does not affect where stress falls'), exceptionless in non-tonal words; no secondary stress. A separate contrastive (lexical, privative H) pitch accent docks on the rightmost non-final vocalic mora; since tone and stress must coincide, tonal words ending in a short vowel have penultimate stress (tone-triggered stress shift), while tonal words ending in a long vowel keep final stress with H on the first mora.
1797.srule: None: the source states there is no secondary stress ('main word stress is final and there is no evidence of secondary stress', p.591; 'there are no secondary or alternating accents', p.638). (Penultimate stress in H-toned words ending in a short vowel is a shift of the single primary stress, see prule/exq_, not a secondary stress.)

1797.tone: Uspanteko 'is unique among the K'ichean languages in having innovated a system of contrastive pitch accent, which operates alongside a separate system of non-contrastive stress' (abstract, p.589). Single privative H tone restricted to the penultimate vocalic mora of the word; 'pitch accent must fall on a stressed syllable' and 'cannot fall on a final mora', which 'derive default final stress, as well as a regular pattern of tone-triggered stress shift'. Presence of H is lexical/morphological ('pitch accent is closely tied to morphology'), its position is surface-phonological. Many words are non-tonal with plain final stress (p.593: 'there are many words with regular final stress and no independent specification of word-level tone').

tn.quote: Beginning with the tonal inventory, we depart from previous treatments of Uspanteko in assuming that all surface tones are the expression of a single, privative, high tone pitch accent. (2) Uspanteko tone is a privative high tone ... This contrasts with Grimes (1971), Campbell (1977), and Can Pixabaj (2006), who each propose that there are two distinct tones in Uspanteko. ... We take the tone-bearing unit (TBU) for Uspanteko to be the vocalic mora (μV) ... We further assume that the H tone of Uspanteko can only appear on a non-word-final TBU

Long (CVV) syllable is stressed 'above all else'; a closed (CVC) syllable 'will be stressed over an open one'; the middle tier -- fortis onset (aspirated plosive / voiceless nasal) 'will usually top a tenuis onset' -- is an ONSET-strength factor, not rhyme weight.

1801.prule: Default: penultimate stress in disyllables; initial stress in morphologically simple trisyllabic nouns (native phonological words have at most three syllables); longer (morphologically complex) words stress the penultimate stress-bearing unit. Overridden by a weight/strength hierarchy: long vowel > fortis (aspirated/voiceless) onset > closed syllable > penultimate position ('a long syllable will be stressed above all else'). Ch. 1 summary: 'Stress is mostly penultimate, with some influence of syllable weight, syllable position in the word, and (g-)wordhood status.'

1802.tone: Register-tone language: three phonemic syllable 'tones' from features HIGH and LONG (never both), with tone sandhi ([+HIGH] lost before [+HIGH]/[+LONG]). No other word-level secondary stress (pretonic 'longueur secondaire' is phonemic vowel length; internal 'accents de soutien' belong to rhythmic groups in connected speech).

evidence_works.work: Thompson 1984-85 [1965], A Vietnamese Grammar (Mon-Khmer Studies 13-14: 1-367)
evidence_works.detail: Treats stress as a 'minor system' of three gradations of syllable force (heavy, medium, weak; §2.14 p.20, §2.7 p.39) distributed over pause groups, not words: 'In ordinary speech the majority of syllables are accompanied by medium stress. In sequences of several such syllables alternate ones are slightly louder, but this is not a distinctive matter. Each pause group has at least one heavy stress.' (§2.72 p.41); 'every pause group has at least one heavy stress' (§2.9 p.50); heavy vs weak stress is assigned by information load ('Emphatic Patterning is the system by which stresses are distributed in pause groups and sentences', §12.5 p.287); pseudo-compounds 'for the most part... have medium stress on each syllable. When they have heavy stress, it generally falls on the final syllable' (p.134). No fixed word-level stress position is posited; the rhythmic alternation is explicitly non-distinctive.

evidence_works.work: Trần 1969, Stress, tones and intonation in South Vietnamese (PhD thesis, Australian National University: 479 pp.)
evidence_works.detail: Finds stress in South Vietnamese sub-phonemic and predictable at the pause-group level: 'The Stress phenomena in South Vietnamese were found to be largely etic and predictable.' (Precis p.1); 'the analysis of stress as presented here refers to a sub-phonemic, and not a phonemic, level. Nearly all the features of Vietnamese stress are predictable in terms of pauses and the rhythm pattern.' (p.98); 'I do not consider relative stress to be phonemically relevant for Vietnamese in view of the fact stated earlier in the study that - apart from the emphatic stress - the occurrence of these relative degrees of stress is predictable in terms of pauses and of the syntactic function of the last syllable of the pause group.' (p.105; she then doubts Thompson's 'three phonemic stress contours' (morendo, sustinendo, crescendo) and holds that 'the contours described by Thompson are a regular feature of individual tones', pp.105-106). The rhythm is retrograde: 'it is the last syllable before the pause which determines the stress pattern of the entire group' with strong and weak stresses alternating back from it (p.109), the pause-group-final syllable being strong or weak by 'the syntactic nature' of that syllable (p.110); 'All words occurring in isolation have a strong stress.' and 'In two syllable utterances, the strong and weak stress alternate.' (p.112), the pause-final syllable is weak under Stress Pattern 1 ('The pattern which starts (when counting regressively) with a weak stress', p.113: onomatopoeic words, reduplicated words of identical syllable structure, verb + final particle, verb + modifier) and strong under Stress Pattern 2 ('The reverse pattern, which begins (when counting regressively) with a strong stress', p.114: reduplicated words of non-identical syllable structure, compounds, noun phrases such as noun+noun/verb and noun+demonstrative). Measured: syllable intensity (stress defined as physical intensity), auditory analysis checked instrumentally, on South Vietnamese pause groups of one to five syllables.

1816.dq: Every word in the language bears one primary stress; in sufficiently long words secondary stress may appear as well. (p.92); tokens measured are 'phrase-medial followed immediately by another word within the phrase' (p.93-94), i.e. word stress explicitly separated from phrase-final effects.
1816.prule: Lexically determined primary stress (marked by an underlying diacritic), restricted to a right-aligned three-syllable window (final/penult/antepenult) in monomorphemic forms; penultimate is the default for lexically unmarked words (~2/3 of lexicon), final ~22%, antepenult ~12%; secondary stress alternates leftward (trochaic); antepenult-stressed 3-4 syllable words shift primary stress to the stem-final syllable before enclitics.
1816.srule: Secondary stress on alternating syllables to the left of the primary stress (trochaic), audible on words of three or more syllables and 'almost always predictable'; at most one secondary stress per monomorphemic or encliticized word (five-syllable àparápiri keeps a final lapse rather than add a third stress); one lexical exception, sivererei 'star' (§3.6.6).
1816.quote: §3.1 (p.92): 'Wamesa is a stress accent language (as opposed to tone or pitch-accent). Every word in the language bears one primary stress; in sufficiently long words secondary stress may appear as well. ... the basic stress pattern of the language, which is lexically determined but always appears within a word-final threesyllable stress window.' §3.2.1 (p.93): 'Wamesa has no lexical tone. Wamesa stress placement is lexically determined and not predictable. The sole restriction is that in monomorphemic forms, primary stress always occurs within a three-syllable window at the end of the stem .…

1819.prule: Stress placement is grammatically (morphologically) determined by two counts: stem syllables carry alternating stress starting with the FIRST stem syllable (odd-numbered from the left of the stem), and suffixal syllables carry alternating stress counting BACKWARD from a final unstressed syllable (even-numbered from the right of the suffix train); special rules apply where the two trains meet at the stem boundary and in suffixless words, and stress placement is phonemically contrastive. Pike 1964 (carried via StressTyp2): 'Stem: every odd syllable from the beginning; Suffixes: every even syllable counting from the end of the word, until the stem or the fourth syllable is reached'; enclitics do not count; clash/lapse repair at the stem-suffix boundary. No weight conditioning; which of the several stresses is primary is not designated by Saint & Pike (p.20: 'The second of two stressed vowels initial in a phonemic word is slightly the more intense of the two').
1819.srule: Several stresses per word, all placed by the two trains given under Primary (stem: 1st, 3rd... stem syllable; suffixes: final unstressed, penult, 4th-from-end... stressed, back to the stem or the 4th syllable; junction rules). The sources rank none of them as primary vs secondary: Pike 1964 treats every stress as one stress phoneme, the last of two or more in the phonemic phrase (word plus enclitics) being 'often freely - not necessarily - weakened' (Rule 4A); Saint & Pike 1962:20: 'The second of two stressed vowels initial in a phonemic word is slightly the more intense of the two'.

1820.prule: Foot (= phonological word: stem plus prestem/poststem affixes and clitics, 1-8 morphemes) carries one primary stress on the final syllable if that syllable is heavy (anything other than V or CV, i.e. closed CVC/VC or complex-nucleus CVV/VV: long vowel or a-diphthong); otherwise on the penult. The same rule assigns each polysyllabic morpheme its own (weaker) stress.
1820.srule: Tracy 1972 uses no term 'secondary stress' and describes no rhythmic stress. Below the word's single primary stress she describes only weaker 'morpheme stress': each morpheme of two or more syllables is stressed on its final syllable unless that syllable is V or CV (then the penult); consonant-only and monosyllabic V/CV morphemes are unstressed; epenthetic syllables are also stressed, and 'all the stresses in the foot except the last are reduced', the last being the primary, 'more pronounced than morpheme stress'.

evidence_works.detail: Brazilian-side Wapichana (Malacacheta and Pium, Roraima), five named speakers (p. 19); recordings analysed with the SIL CECIL/Spectrum package (p. 19-20), which supplies loudness/intensity and VOT traces. Santos states no stress rule of his own and gives stress only in passing, but two first-hand passages sit with the entry's coding: (i) p. 62, on VOT of [k]/[g] in [akaj] 'fruta' and [pigaɾ] 'tu', the environment is described as 'sílaba tônica de final de palavra, iniciando sílaba pesada cuja rima começa pela vogal [a]' -- word-final stress on a heavy (closed) syllable, as Tracy's final-unless-V/CV rule predicts; (ii) p. 103-104, syncope /usakãntãn/ -> [oskãntãn] 'ela sentou-se', where the intensity trace shows the abstract syllable /sa/ with minimal intensity rise, characterised as a post-lexical phonetic rule acting 'em sílabas átonas de palavras com mais de duas sílabas' -- weak pre-tonic syllables in a word with final stress. (iii) p. 98 and p. 108-109: syllable inventory of Clements & Keyser type 4 (CV, V, CVC, VC) with branching nuclei allowed except VVC, the closed types explicitly called 'sílabas pesadas' -- independent support for the entry's heavy/light split (V and CV light, everything else heavy). p. 108 says the processes found 'ratificam as afirmações de Tracy (1972)'.

1821.dq: Suprasegmental phenomena such as pitch accent, tone, or contrastive stress do not play a role in Warembori. ... Stress is normally assigned to the penultimate syllable of a word or compound. ... In terms of stress assignment, then, the compounds of Warembori do not behave as single phonological words for stress assignment, but neither do they behave as two totally independent words.

1822.dq: Stress assignment is determined by the position of the syllable in the phonological and prosodic word. ... A syllable that does not have any weak branches up to the phonological word receives primary stress (this is always, and only, the initial syllable of a phonological word ...)
1822.dloc: ch. 2 Phonetics and phonology, sec. 2.6 Prosody / 2.6.1 Stress, pp. 49-52 (incl. fn. 4 p. 50)
1822.prule: Primary stress always and only on the initial syllable of the phonological word (quantity-insensitive, independent of syllable count; one known lexical exception mayi'patturla). Word-final syllables are never stressed and adjacent syllables cannot both be stressed. Analysis after Warlpiri (Nash 1986; Pentland & Laughren 2004): disyllabic feet built first-to-last within each prosodic word, stray syllable adjoined to the preceding foot, strong-weak labelling with leftmost strong.
1822.srule: Secondary stress on the first (strong) syllable of every non-initial foot: disyllabic feet are built first-to-last within each prosodic word and a leftover syllable joins the preceding foot, so no word-final and no adjacent stresses (minija: initial stress only; ('Jampi)(jinpa)). Suffixes and clitics of two or more syllables form a new prosodic word and take secondary stress on their first syllable ('maliki,kuma 'dog-AVER'); monosyllabic affixes are footed with the stem ('mali,ku-rlu 'dog-ERG', secondary on the third syllable).
1822.quote: The basic patterns of stress in Warlmanpa are: a) disyllabic morphemes (including roots) receive stress on their initial syllable; b) adjacent syllables cannot both be stressed; and c) word-final syllables cannot be stressed. ... Stress assignment is determined by the position of the syllable in the phonological and prosodic word. Syllables are assigned to feet, where each disyllable in a prosodic word constitutes a well-formed foot, from first to last ... 1823.prule: Penultimate stress. Mead (1998:97) states it without hedge as a property of all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages; Waru is one of the 15 languages of Mead's own survey (Waru and Lalomerui word lists 61-62 elicited by Mead himself, 30 Nov 1988, graded 'very good'), so the statement covers Waru from first-hand data. Mead 1999 App. 3 restates it as the reading default for the 27 selected word lists (Waru/WAR among them): penultimate stress on the next-to-last written vowel unless marked; no stress-marked WAR items are visible (scan caveat: diacritics may be lost in scan). Syllables are only V/CV, no phonemic vowel length (phonetic long vowels = two like vowels, each written and counted), so weight plays no role. No Waru-specific phonology or grammar exists (Glottolog lists only Mead 1998, Mead 2024 Oxford Guide chapter, ELCat 2022).
